docs.title: OromScript
docs.text:
Write Python in Afan Oromo — Execute Anywhere

OromScript is an open-source, language-localisation transpiler platform that lets developers write Python programs using Afan Oromo keywords, identifiers, and idioms.

The transpiler parses Oromo-syntax source files (.orm), translates them into standard Python (3.10 or newer), and executes or outputs the result — with no measurable runtime overhead above Python itself.

docs.title: Core Value Proposition
docs.text: Lower the barrier to programming for the 40+ million Afan Oromo speakers worldwide. It also provides a reusable, well-documented platform so any other language community (Amharic, Tigrinya, Somali, etc.) can add their own keyword layer seamlessly.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Full Python Parity: Every Python 3 construct has an Afan Oromo equivalent.
  • Zero Runtime Overhead: Generated Python is fully identical to hand-written Python. CPython runs the output directly.
  • Language Plugin Architecture: Add a new language by simply supplying one JSON keyword map.
  • Hand-written Lexer and Parser: The lexer and the recursive descent parser are part of this project, not wrappers around Python's tokenize module. f-strings are parsed by the same code, including = debug fields, conversions and nested format specs. They keep the line and column of your original .orm source, so errors point at what you wrote.
  • Afan Oromo Aware: Words with a hudhaa, such as walitti_ida'i, work with a straight or curly apostrophe. Names inside f-strings are translated too. oromscript.graphemes knows the letters of Afan Oromo: digraphs (dh), long vowels (aa), doubled consonants (bb) and the hudhaa. The parser attaches these as Grapheme nodes to every name in the tree (node.graphemes), and split_graphemes / grapheme_len work on plain words.
  • VS Code Support: Syntax highlighting extension included.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
To view examples, check out the examples/ directory containing concepts like loops, conditional statements, simple scripts, classes and match/case scenarios.

oromscript run examples/hello_world.orm
oromscript run examples/fibonacci.orm

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
• The lexer and parser are tested against CPython itself: same syntax tree, same node positions, and the same accept/reject decisions on hundreds of snippets and on the Python standard library.
  • Memory tests run the whole pipeline many times and fail if memory or live object counts grow.
  • python benchmarks/bench.py reports time per stage, tokens per second, and memory growth. On a development laptop the lexer and parser handle about 230,000 to 330,000 tokens per second. The parse stage of a 1 MB file takes 0.25 to 0.45 seconds, and the whole transpile (with semantic analysis and code generation) about 1.2 to 1.3 seconds.

OROMSCRIPT

Transpiler Design Specification

Write Python in Afan Oromo — Execute Anywhere

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Version 1.0 · May 2025 · Open Source (MIT)

github.com/ayanasamuel8/transpiler-afan-oromo-script

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
OromScript is an open-source, language-localisation transpiler platform that lets developers write Python programs using Afan Oromo keywords, identifiers, and idioms. The transpiler parses Oromo-syntax source files (.orm), translates them into standard Python, and executes or outputs the result — with no measurable runtime overhead above Python itself.

Core value proposition: lower the barrier to programming for the 40+ million Afan Oromo speakers worldwide, and provide a reusable, well-documented platform so any other language community (Amharic, Tigrinya, Somali, …) can add their own keyword layer in under a day.

Scope boundaries (what this design covers) • Afan Oromo → Python 3.10 or newer full-language transpiler (all Python constructs) • A plugin/adapter system for adding new languages (Amharic, etc.) • CLI tool, library API, VS Code syntax highlighting extension • Comprehensive test suite, CI/CD pipeline, contribution workflow • Localized error messages in Oromo (and extensible for other languages) • NOT in scope for v1: JIT compilation, custom C-extension ABI, IDE debugger protocol

docs.title: 2.1 Goals
docs.text: Priority Goal P0 Full Python parity — every Python 3 construct has an Afan Oromo equivalent P0 Transpile-time only overhead; generated Python must be identical to hand-written Python P0 Plugin architecture: add a new language by supplying one JSON keyword map + optional grammar hooks P1 Localized, actionable error messages (line/col, suggestion, Oromo text) P1 VS Code extension with syntax highlighting for .orm files P1 CI/CD with automated tests, linting, and release publishing P2 Source-map support so stack traces reference .orm lines P2 REPL (interactive Oromo Python shell)

docs.title: 2.2 Non-Goals (v1)
docs.text:
• Custom bytecode compiler or JIT — Python's CPython handles execution

  • Full IDE debugger (DAP) integration — deferred to v2

  • Transpiling to languages other than Python — possible in v2 via IR

  • GUI application — CLI + library is sufficient for v1

docs.title: 3. Architecture Overview
docs.text:
OromScript follows a classic multi-phase compiler pipeline. The key design decision is to keep the Oromo-specific logic (lexer keyword map, grammar patches) strictly isolated from the generic AST manipulation and Python code-generation layers. This is what enables easy addition of new languages.

Figure 1 — High-level transpiler pipeline

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ OROMSCRIPT PIPELINE │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ .orm source file │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ keyword_map.json ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ LEXER │◄─────────────────────│ Language Adapter (Oromo) │ │ (Tokenizer)│ │ • keyword_map.json │ └─────────────┘ │ • grammar_hooks.py (opt.) │ │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ token stream ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ PARSER │ (Python grammar extended with adapter hooks) │ (recursive descent) │ └─────────────┘ │ │ AST (language-neutral) ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ SEMANTIC │ (symbol table, scope, type hints validation) │ ANALYSER │ └─────────────┘ │ │ annotated AST ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ CODE GEN │ ast.unparse() → standard Python source │ + SOURCEMAP│ produces .py + .orm.map (line/col mapping) └─────────────┘ │ ├── output.py (for --emit-python) └──► CPython (for --run)

docs.title: 3.1 Language Adapter (Plugin) Concept
docs.text:
A Language Adapter is the only artefact a contributor needs to create to localise the platform for a new language. It consists of:

  • keyword_map.json — maps every Python keyword / builtin to the local-language equivalent

  • grammar_hooks.py (optional) — Python module with hooks if the language needs non-trivial grammar extensions (e.g. right-to-left parsing, agglutinative morphology)

  • error_messages.json — localised error strings keyed by error code

  • tests/ — adapter-specific test corpus

Figure 2 — Language Adapter file structure

adapters/ ├── afan_oromo/ ← shipped with this repo │ ├── keyword_map.json │ ├── grammar_hooks.py │ ├── error_messages.json │ └── tests/ └── amharic/ ← future adapter (community-contributed) ├── keyword_map.json └── ...

docs.title: 3.2 Why Python as the IR (Intermediate Representation)
docs.text:
Rather than designing a custom IR, v1 uses Python source text as the IR. This gives us:

  • Zero execution overhead — CPython runs the output directly

  • Full ecosystem compatibility — pip packages, type checkers, debuggers all work

  • Simpler code generator — we use Python's built-in ast.unparse()

  • Easy verification — diff the generated .py against expected output in tests

Future IR note (v2 consideration) If the project later targets multiple backends (JavaScript, Rust, etc.), a proper IR (e.g. LLVM or a custom DAG) can be introduced between the Semantic Analyser and Code Gen layers without touching the Lexer, Parser, or Adapter.

docs.title: 4.1 Lexer
docs.text:
The Lexer is hand-written. It reads the source with one compiled regular expression, tracks indentation itself, and applies a reverse keyword map: any name token whose text matches a local-language keyword or builtin is replaced with the corresponding Python name before the parser sees it. It emits standard tokenize.TokenInfo objects, so the parser always works with standard Python tokens and needs no changes per language.

Beyond keyword translation, the Lexer:

  • keeps the line and column of the original .orm text on every token, so errors point at what the user wrote
  • translates names inside the {...} fields of f-strings, and leaves literal text and format specifications alone
  • matches keywords that contain a hudhaa (apostrophe), such as walitti_ida'i, and accepts the curly apostrophes ’, ʼ and ‘ for them (see oromscript/graphemes.py)
  • raises OrmLexError (code E0001) for an unterminated string, an invalid character, an unclosed bracket, or inconsistent indentation
# oromscript/lexer.py (simplified) class OrmLexer: def __init__(self, source, adapter): self._combined_map \= {local: python for python, local in adapter.maps()} self._scanner \= _build_scanner(adapter) # one compiled regex def tokenize(self): tokens \= [] while pos \< len(source): match \= self._scanner.match(source, pos) # string, number, name, operator, comment, newline ... # INDENT/DEDENT are emitted at the start of each logical line if match.lastgroup \== "name": text \= self._combined_map.get(text, text) tokens.append(TokenInfo(...)) return tokens

docs.title: 4.2 Parser
docs.text:
The parser is a hand-written recursive descent parser. It reads the translated token list and builds a standard Python ast tree directly, with line and column numbers on every node. f-strings are cut into text and fields by oromscript/fstrings.py and each field is read by the same parser. The parser also attaches Grapheme nodes (the digraphs, long vowels, doubled consonants and hudhaa of each name) to every name node as node.graphemes; they are not part of _fields, so Python's tools and compile ignore them. Expressions use precedence climbing. Each statement kind has its own method. match and case are soft keywords, so the parser tries a match statement first and falls back to a normal name.

Because the output is a standard Python AST, the semantic analyser and ast.unparse() work unchanged. The parser is tested against CPython's own ast.parse (same tree, same positions, same accept/reject decisions) on hundreds of snippets and on the Python standard library.

Grammar hooks in the adapter can pre-process the source string for languages with structural differences (e.g. postfix function calls). A hook receives the translated source text. If it changes the text, that text is parsed with Python's ast.parse. If it returns the text unchanged, the hand-written parser is used.

docs.title: 4.3 Semantic Analyser
docs.text:
The semantic analyser performs a single-pass walk of the AST to:

  • Build a symbol table (scoped dictionary of names → type hints)

  • Validate that all referenced names are defined (optional strict mode)

  • Annotate nodes with source-map information (original .orm line/col)

  • Detect common localisation mistakes (e.g., mixing Oromo and Python keywords)

docs.title: 4.4 Code Generator
docs.text:
The code generator calls ast.unparse(tree) to produce Python source from the annotated AST. It also emits a JSON source-map file (.orm.map) mapping every generated line back to the original Oromo source line, enabling localised stack traces.

# oromscript/codegen.py import ast, json class CodeGen: def generate(self, tree: ast.AST, source_map: dict) -> tuple[str, str]: py_source \= ast.unparse(tree) map_json \= json.dumps(source_map, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) return py_source, map_json

docs.title: 4.5 Error Reporting
docs.text:
Errors are structured objects carrying a numeric code, the offending .orm line/col, and a localised message. The error renderer looks up the message template from the active adapter's error_messages.json and formats it with context-specific substitution variables.

Figure 3 — Error message flow

OromSyntaxError(code=E0042, line=7, col=3, context={'token': 'yoo'}) │ ▼ ErrorRenderer(adapter='afan_oromo') │ looks up error_messages.json[E0042] │ template: "Wardii himaa '{token}' iddoo dha'uu hin qabu — sarara {line}" ▼ stderr: error[E0042] sarara 7, tuqaa 3: Wardii himaa 'yoo' iddoo dha'uu hin qabu — sarara 7 Yaadannoo: 'yoo' jechuun 'if' jechuu dha; akka armaan gadiitti fayyadami: yoo gatii > 0:

docs.title: 4.6 Adapter Registry
docs.text:
The AdapterRegistry discovers adapters at startup by scanning the adapters/ directory for subdirectories containing a keyword_map.json. Adapters can also be installed as PyPI packages following the naming convention oromscript-lang-\<name>, allowing community adapters to be distributed independently.

# oromscript/adapter.py class AdapterRegistry: _adapters: dict[str, Adapter] \= {} @classmethod def discover(cls, adapters_dir: Path): for d in adapters_dir.iterdir(): if (d / 'keyword_map.json').exists(): cls._adapters[d.name] \= Adapter.load(d) @classmethod def get(cls, lang: str) -> Adapter: if lang not in cls._adapters: raise AdapterNotFoundError(lang) return cls._adapters[lang]

docs.title: 4.7 CLI Interface
docs.text:
The command-line interface is built with Click and supports:

# Usage examples oromscript run hello.orm # transpile + execute oromscript compile hello.orm # emit hello.py oromscript compile hello.orm --map # emit hello.py + hello.orm.map oromscript check hello.orm # lint only, no output oromscript repl # interactive Oromo Python REPL oromscript new-lang amharic # scaffold a new adapter oromscript --lang amharic run hi.amh # use a different adapter

docs.title: 4.8 Library API
docs.text:
OromScript is importable as a Python library so it can be embedded in notebooks, build tools, or web services:

from oromscript import transpile, execute py_source \= transpile('agarsiisi("Akkam!")', lang='afan_oromo') result \= execute('agarsiisi("Akkam!")', lang='afan_oromo')

docs.title: 5. Keyword Map Design
docs.text:
The keyword map is the heart of each language adapter. It is a UTF-8 JSON file with two top-level objects: keywords and builtins.

// adapters/afan_oromo/keyword_map.json (excerpt) { "$schema": "https://oromscript.dev/schemas/keyword_map/v1.json", "$lang": "afan_oromo", "$version": "1.0.0", "$description": "Afan Oromo keyword mapping for OromScript", "keywords": { "if": "yoo", "else": "yoo_miti", "elif": "yookaan", "for": "hanga", "while": "yeroo", "def": "hojii", "class": "gosa", "return": "deebi", "import": "fidi", "from": "irra", "as": "akka", "try": "yaali", "except": "dogoggora", "finally": "dhuma", "with": "waliin", "pass": "itti_fufuu", "break": "addaan_kut", "continue": "itti_fufuu", "and": "fi", "or": "yookaan", "not": "miti", "in": "keessa", "is": "dha", "lambda": "hanga", "True": "Dhugaa", "False": "Sobaa", "None": "Wanti_hin_jirre" }, "builtins": { "print": "agarsiisi", "input": "gaafadhu", "len": "dheerina", "range": "lakkoofsa", "list": "tarree", "dict": "galmee", "str": "barruu", "int": "lakki", "float": "lakki_caccabaa", "open": "bani" } }

The schema at oromscript.dev/schemas/keyword_map/v1.json enforces this structure and is validated in CI. Adding a new keyword requires: (1) add entry to keyword_map.json, (2) add a test case, (3) open a PR.

Design rule: 1-to-1 mapping only in v1 Each Python keyword maps to exactly one local keyword, and each local keyword maps to exactly one Python keyword. Many-to-one mappings (synonyms) are deferred to v2 to keep the lexer translation logic O(1) and deterministic.

docs.title: 6.1 Hello World
docs.text: Afan Oromo (.orm) # Baga nagaan dhufte! agarsiisi("Akkam, Addunyaa!") Generated Python (.py) # Baga nagaan dhufte! print("Akkam, Addunyaa!")

docs.title: 6.2 Functions and Conditionals
docs.text: Afan Oromo (.orm) hojii faarfannaa(lakki):     yoo lakki % 2 \== 0:         deebi 'lakkoofsa lakkaa'     yoo_miti:         deebi 'lakkoofsa baayyee' hanga i keessa lakkoofsa(1, 11):     agarsiisi(faarfannaa(i)) Generated Python (.py) def faarfannaa(lakki):     if lakki % 2 \== 0:         return 'lakkoofsa lakkaa'     else:         return 'lakkoofsa baayyee' for i in range(1, 11):     print(faarfannaa(i))

docs.title: 6.3 Classes
docs.text: Afan Oromo (.orm) gosa Barataa:     hojii __init__(of, maqaa, umri):         of.maqaa \= maqaa         of.umri  \= umri     hojii of_ibsi(of):         agarsiisi(f'{of.maqaa}: {of.umri}') b \= Barataa('Chaltu', 20) b.of_ibsi() Generated Python (.py) class Barataa:     def __init__(self, maqaa, umri):         self.maqaa \= maqaa         self.umri  \= umri     def of_ibsi(self):         print(f'{self.maqaa}: {self.umri}') b \= Barataa('Chaltu', 20) b.of_ibsi() Note on 'self' In the Afan Oromo adapter, 'self' is mapped to 'of' (meaning 'itself' / 'oneself' in Oromo). The keyword_map.json entry is: "self": "of". Adapter authors can choose any culturally appropriate equivalent.

docs.title: 8. Performance Strategy
docs.text: The performance goal is that OromScript programs run indistinguishably from equivalent hand-written Python. This is achievable because the transpiler is a one-time preprocessing step — not an interpreter.

docs.title: 8.1 Transpilation Speed
docs.text:
Operation Method Measured, 1000-line file Tokenise + keyword translation Hand-written regex lexer, O(1) dict lookup per name about 7 ms Parse Hand-written recursive descent parser about 7 ms Semantic analysis AST visitor about 2 ms Code gen ast.unparse() (CPython) about 13 ms Total transpile — about 30 ms (budget: 100 ms)

These are measured on a development laptop with Python 3.14 (5,000 tokens). A 1 MB file (175,000 tokens) transpiles in about 1.2 to 1.3 seconds. The lexer and parser together handle 230,000 to 330,000 tokens per second, and the parse stage of a 1 MB file takes 0.25 to 0.45 seconds. python benchmarks/bench.py --ci fails if a budget is missed or if throughput falls below 15,000 tokens per second.

docs.title: 8.2 Runtime Performance
docs.text:
• Generated .py is byte-for-byte equivalent to hand-written Python → CPython compiles it identically → zero runtime overhead

  • Source-map JSON generation is optional (--map flag) and happens post-transpile

  • Caching: oromscript run caches compiled .pyc next to the .orm file (in __pycache__) and skips re-transpilation if the .orm mtime has not changed — identical to how Python's own import cache works

docs.title: 8.3 Future: C Extension Option
docs.text:
If transpilation speed ever becomes a bottleneck (e.g. transpiling thousands of files in a CI build), the lexer and parser can be re-implemented as a C extension using CPython's C API. The interface is already designed with this in mind: OromLexer exposes a single tokenize() method and OrmParser a single parse() method, and their return types would not change.

Guideline Do not pre-optimise. Measure first with benchmarks/bench.py. The pure-Python lexer and parser are the v1 baseline; a C extension is a v2 option only if benchmarks show a real bottleneck.

docs.title: 9. Adding a New Language (Amharic Example)
docs.text:
This section is a step-by-step guide for a contributor who wants to add an Amharic adapter. The same steps apply to any language.

  1. Scaffold the adapter directory:
oromscript new-lang amharic # Creates: adapters/amharic/keyword_map.json (template) # adapters/amharic/error_messages.json (template) # adapters/amharic/grammar_hooks.py (no-op stub) # adapters/amharic/tests/
  1. Fill in keyword_map.json with Amharic equivalents:
// adapters/amharic/keyword_map.json (excerpt) { "$lang": "amharic", "keywords": { "if": "ከሆነ", "else": "ካልሆነ", "for": "ለ", "def": "ሥራ", "class": "ዓይነት", "return":"መልስ" }, "builtins": { "print": "አሳይ", "input": "ጠይቅ" } }

  1. Add error messages in error_messages.json (Amharic text)

  2. Add test corpus: pairs of .amh + expected .py files in adapters/amharic/tests/corpus/

  3. Run tests:

pytest adapters/amharic/tests/ -v
  1. Validate keyword map schema:
oromscript validate-adapter adapters/amharic/
  1. Open a Pull Request — CI will run schema validation + tests automatically
Time estimate A complete, tested adapter for a new language typically takes 4–8 hours: • 2 h — keyword translation (using a dictionary or LLM assistance) • 1 h — error message localisation • 2 h — writing test corpus • 1 h — PR + review cycle

docs.title: 11.1 Test layers
docs.text: Layer What is tested Tool Unit Lexer tokens and positions, parser trees, graphemes, adapter loading, error formatting pytest Differential Lexer and parser agree with CPython's tokenize and ast.parse (trees, positions, accept/reject) pytest Memory Repeated runs do not grow memory or object counts pytest + tracemalloc Integration Full .orm → .py round-trip for every keyword pytest + corpus Execution .orm programs produce correct stdout/return values pytest + subprocess Performance Transpile time within budget; throughput of at least 15,000 tokens/sec; time grows linearly pytest + benchmarks/bench.py Schema Every keyword_map.json validates against JSON Schema jsonschema CLI

docs.title: 11.2 Corpus test format
docs.text:
Each integration test is a pair of files:

adapters/afan_oromo/tests/corpus/ ├── 001_hello.orm # Oromo source ├── 001_hello.py # Expected Python output ├── 002_for_loop.orm ├── 002_for_loop.py └── ...

The test runner transpiles each .orm and diffs the output against the .py reference. Any diff is a test failure. New contributors adding keywords must add at least one corpus pair.

docs.title: 11.3 Coverage requirement
docs.text:
• Core engine: ≥ 90% line coverage (enforced in CI via pytest-cov)

  • Adapter keyword_map.json: 100% of keywords must have at least one corpus test

  • Error paths: every error code must have a test that triggers it

docs.title: 12. Contribution Workflow
docs.text:

docs.title: 14. Versioning & Release
docs.text: OromScript follows Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0). The Python package, VS Code extension, and keyword_map.json schema are versioned independently but co-released.

docs.title: 14.1 Version matrix
docs.text: Version bump Trigger Examples PATCH (x.y.Z) Bug fix, docs, no API change Fix wrong keyword mapping MINOR (x.Y.0) New keyword, new feature, backward-compatible Add 10 new builtins MAJOR (X.0.0) Breaking change to public API or keyword_map schema Rename a keyword, schema v2

docs.title: 14.2 Release steps (automated via release.yml)
docs.text:
1. Maintainer creates and pushes a tag: git tag v1.2.3 && git push --tags

  2. release.yml triggers; builds wheel + sdist

  3. Publishes to PyPI via OIDC trusted publishing (no stored secrets)

  4. Builds VS Code .vsix and publishes to Marketplace

  5. Creates GitHub Release with auto-generated notes from CHANGELOG.md

docs.title: 16. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• No code execution during transpilation: the transpiler only parses and transforms ASTs — it never eval()s user code

  • Dependency minimisation: core library has zero runtime dependencies beyond Python stdlib — reduces supply chain attack surface

  • Sandboxed execution: oromscript run does not grant any additional permissions beyond what python itself would; the generated .py runs in a normal CPython process

  • JSON Schema validation: keyword_map.json is schema-validated before loading — prevents malformed adapter files from causing unexpected behaviour

  • No network access during transpile: the transpiler is fully offline; no telemetry, no update checks

docs.title: Adding a Language
docs.text: OromScript is designed to support arbitrary spoken languages via an Adapter System. Adapters are lightweight JSON definitions that map Python language structures to local language words.

docs.title: Creating an Adapter
docs.text:
1. Inside the adapters/ folder, create a new directory for your language (e.g., adapters/amharic/).
  2. Inside that directory, create a keyword_map.json file.
  3. Map Python keywords to your target language:
{
  "$schema": "https://oromscript.dev/schemas/keyword_map/v1.json",
  "$lang": "amharic",
  "$version": "1.0.0",
  "keywords": {
    "def": "tegbari",
    "if": "kehone",
    "print": "atmi"
  },
  "builtins": {
    "str": "tsehufe"
  }
}

docs.title: Validating the Adapter
docs.text:
You can use the built-in validator to ensure your schema is correct: 

oromscript validate-adapter adapters/amharic/

@main.command()
@click.argument("file", type=click.Path(exists=True, path_type=Path))
@click.option("--lang", default="afan_oromo", show_default=True)
@click.option("--map", "emit_map", is_flag=True)
@click.option("-o", "--output", type=click.Path(path_type=Path))
@click.option("--stdout", is_flag=True)
def compile(
    file: Path, lang: str, emit_map: bool, output: Path | None, stdout: bool
) -> None:
    """Transpile FILE to Python source."""
    source = file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    try:
        result = transpile(source, lang=lang, emit_map=emit_map)
    except OrmError as e:
        click.echo(str(e), err=True)
        sys.exit(1)

    if isinstance(result, tuple):
        py_src, map_json = result
    else:
        py_src, map_json = result, None

    if stdout:
        click.echo(py_src)
        return
    out_path = output or file.with_suffix(".py")
    out_path.write_text(py_src, encoding="utf-8")
    click.echo(f"✓ Written: {out_path}")
    if map_json and emit_map:
        map_path = file.with_suffix(".orm.map")
        map_path.write_text(map_json, encoding="utf-8")
        click.echo(f"✓ Written: {map_path}")

def transpile(
    source: str,
    lang: str = "afan_oromo",
    strict: bool = False,
    emit_map: bool = False,
) -> str | tuple[str, str]:
    """Transpile localised source to Python source.

    Args:
        source:    Raw source text in the local language.
        lang:      Language adapter to use (default: 'afan_oromo').
        strict:    Enable strict name checking.
        emit_map:  If True, also return source-map JSON.

    Returns:
        py_source if emit_map is False, else (py_source, map_json).
    """
    adapter = AdapterRegistry.get(lang)
    try:
        tokens = OrmLexer(source, adapter).tokenize()
        tree = OrmParser(adapter).parse(tokens)
        tree, src_map = SemanticAnalyser(source.splitlines(), strict=strict).analyse(
            tree
        )
        py_source, map_json = CodeGen().generate(
            tree, source_map=src_map if emit_map else None
        )
    except RecursionError as exc:
        # Deeply nested code (or a very long chain of operators) can exhaust
        # the stack in the visitors that walk the tree.
        raise OrmSyntaxError(
            code="E0010",
            message="The program is nested too deeply",
            lang=lang,
        ) from exc
    if emit_map:
        return py_source, map_json  # type: ignore[return-value]
    return py_source

docs.title: Lexer
docs.text:
oromscript.lexer ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ A hand-written lexer for Afan Oromo (or any localised) Python source.

It reads the source in one pass with a single compiled regular expression, tracks indentation itself, and replaces local-language names with their Python equivalents. It produces standard tokenize.TokenInfo objects, so other tools can read its output.

This is the first stage of the OromScript transpile pipeline.

class OrmLexer:
    """Tokenise a localised source string and translate it to Python tokens.

    Args:
        source: Raw source text in the target local language.
        adapter: The loaded Adapter for the active language.

    Example::

        lexer = OrmLexer(source, adapter)
        tokens = lexer.tokenize()
    """

    def __init__(self, source: str, adapter: Adapter) -> None:
        self._source = source
        self._adapter = adapter
        forward_map = {
            **adapter.keyword_map,
            **adapter.builtin_map,
        }
        self._combined_map: dict[str, str] = {
            normalize_hudhaa(v): k for k, v in forward_map.items()
        }
        self._scanner = _build_scanner(
            tuple(sorted(w for w in self._combined_map if HUDHAA in w))
        )
        self._name_re = re.compile(_NAME)

    # ── Public API ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    def tokenize(self) -> list[py_tokenize.TokenInfo]:
        """Tokenise the source and return a translated token list.

        Returns:
            List of TokenInfo where local-language NAME tokens have been
            replaced with their Python equivalents. The list always ends
            with NEWLINE (if needed), DEDENT tokens and ENDMARKER.

        Raises:
            OrmLexError: If the source cannot be tokenised.
        """
        with gc_paused():
            return self._tokenize()

    def _tokenize(self) -> list[py_tokenize.TokenInfo]:
        # Python treats \r\n and \r as a newline. Do the same, once.
        source = self._source.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n")
        if source.startswith("\ufeff"):
            source = source[1:]  # a byte order mark is not code
        nul = source.find("\x00")
        if nul >= 0:
            raise self._fail("Lexer error: '\\x00'", source, nul)
        lines = source.split("\n")
        # Each token keeps a reference to its line. Build the texts once, or a
        # very long line would be copied again for every token on it.
        line_texts = [line + "\n" for line in lines]
        if not source.endswith("\n"):
            line_texts[-1] = lines[-1]
        scanner = self._scanner
        mapping = self._combined_map
        tokens: list[py_tokenize.TokenInfo] = []
        append = tokens.append
        TokenInfo = py_tokenize.TokenInfo

        pos = 0
        end = len(source)
        line_no = 1
        line_start = 0
        brackets: list[tuple[str, int, int]] = []  # open brackets: char, line, col
        indents = [0]
        alt_indents = [0]  # the same levels, counting a tab as one column
        at_line_start = True
        pending_newline = False  # a logical line has content but no NEWLINE yet

        while pos < end:
            if at_line_start and not brackets:
                pos, line_no, line_start, blank = self._handle_indent(
                    source,
                    pos,
                    line_no,
                    line_start,
                    line_texts,
                    indents,
                    alt_indents,
                    tokens,
                )
                if blank:
                    # Blank or comment-only line: the helper consumed it.
                    continue
                at_line_start = False

            match = scanner.match(source, pos)
            if match is None:
                self._raise_at(source, pos, line_no, line_start)
            kind = match.lastgroup
            text = match.group()
            col = pos - line_start
            line_text = line_texts[line_no - 1]

            if kind == "ws":
                pos = match.end()
                continue
            if kind == "comment":
                append(
                    TokenInfo(
                        COMMENT,
                        text,
                        (line_no, col),
                        (line_no, col + len(text)),
                        line_text,
                    )
                )
                pos = match.end()
                continue
            if kind == "newline":
                if brackets:
                    append(
                        TokenInfo(
                            NL, "\n", (line_no, col), (line_no, col + 1), line_text
                        )
                    )
                else:
                    if pending_newline:
                        append(
                            TokenInfo(
                                NEWLINE,
                                "\n",
                                (line_no, col),
                                (line_no, col + 1),
                                line_text,
                            )
                        )
                        pending_newline = False
                    at_line_start = True
                pos = match.end()
                line_no += 1
                line_start = pos
                continue
            if kind == "cont":
                pos = match.end()
                if pos >= end:
                    raise self._fail(CONTINUATION_EOF, source, end)
                line_no += 1
                line_start = pos
                continue
            # Real token: the logical line now has content.
            pending_newline = True
            # A single-quoted f-string may hold a newline inside a field (Python
            # 3.12), which the string pattern cannot match. Scan it by hand.
            forced_f = (
                kind == "name"
                and text.lower() in _F_PREFIXES
                and source[match.end() : match.end() + 1] in ("'", '"')
            )
            if kind == "string" or forced_f:
                string_end = match.end()
                if forced_f or _is_fstring(text):
                    string_end, text = self._scan_fstring(source, pos)
                raw_text = source[pos:string_end]
                new_lines = raw_text.count("\n")
                start = (line_no, col)
                if new_lines:
                    last_nl = raw_text.rfind("\n")
                    end_pos = (line_no + new_lines, len(raw_text) - last_nl - 1)
                else:
                    end_pos = (line_no, col + len(raw_text))
                append(TokenInfo(STRING, text, start, end_pos, line_text))
                pos = string_end
                if new_lines:
                    line_no += new_lines
                    line_start = source.rfind("\n", 0, pos) + 1
                continue
            if kind == "number":
                append(
                    TokenInfo(
                        NUMBER,
                        text,
                        (line_no, col),
                        (line_no, col + len(text)),
                        line_text,
                    )
                )
            elif kind == "name" or kind == "hudhaa":
                if kind == "hudhaa":
                    text = normalize_hudhaa(text)
                elif not text.isidentifier():
                    bad = _first_invalid_character(text)
                    self._raise_at(source, pos + bad, line_no, line_start)
                elif not text.isascii():
                    # Python compares identifiers in NFKC form.
                    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)
                py_text = mapping.get(text, text)
                append(
                    TokenInfo(
                        NAME,
                        py_text,
                        (line_no, col),
                        (line_no, col + len(match.group())),
                        line_text,
                    )
                )
            else:  # operator
                if text in _OPENERS:
                    brackets.append((text, line_no, col))
                elif text in _CLOSERS and brackets:
                    brackets.pop()
                append(
                    TokenInfo(
                        OP, text, (line_no, col), (line_no, col + len(text)), line_text
                    )
                )
            pos = match.end()

        return self._finish(tokens, brackets, pending_newline, indents, line_no, lines)

    # ── Indentation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    def _handle_indent(
        self,
        source: str,
        pos: int,
        line_no: int,
        line_start: int,
        line_texts: list[str],
        indents: list[int],
        alt_indents: list[int],
        tokens: list[py_tokenize.TokenInfo],
    ) -> tuple[int, int, int, bool]:
        """Measure the indentation at ``pos`` and emit INDENT/DEDENT tokens.

        Returns ``(pos, line_no, line_start, blank)``. For a code line, ``pos``
        is the first non-blank character. For a blank or comment-only line,
        the line's tokens are emitted, ``blank`` is True and ``pos`` is the
        start of the next line. A backslash at the start of a line counts as
        indentation whitespace, as it does in CPython.
        """
        end = len(source)
        column = 0
        alt_column = 0
        # CPython: a backslash inside the indentation fixes the level at the
        # column of the first backslash that is not at column 0.
        fixed_column = 0
        scan = pos
        while scan < end:
            ch = source[scan]
            if ch == " ":
                column += 1
                alt_column += 1
            elif ch == "\t":
                column = (column // _TAB_SIZE + 1) * _TAB_SIZE
                alt_column += 1
            elif ch == "\f":
                column = alt_column = 0
            elif ch == "\\" and source.startswith("\\\n", scan):
                scan += 1  # the newline is skipped below
                line_no += 1
                line_start = scan + 1
                fixed_column = fixed_column or column
                if line_start >= end:
                    raise self._fail(CONTINUATION_EOF, source, end)
            else:
                break
            scan += 1
        if fixed_column:
            column = alt_column = fixed_column

        line_text = line_texts[line_no - 1]
        if scan >= end or source[scan] in "#\n":
            # Blank line or comment-only line: no INDENT/DEDENT.
            nl_pos = source.find("\n", scan)
            stop = end if nl_pos < 0 else nl_pos
            col = scan - line_start
            if scan < end and source[scan] == "#":
                comment = source[scan:stop]
                tokens.append(
                    py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                        COMMENT,
                        comment,
                        (line_no, col),
                        (line_no, col + len(comment)),
                        line_text,
                    )
                )
                col += len(comment)
            if stop < end:
                tokens.append(
                    py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                        NL, "\n", (line_no, col), (line_no, col + 1), line_text
                    )
                )
            return (stop + 1 if stop < end else end + 1), line_no + 1, stop + 1, True

        if column > indents[-1]:
            if alt_column <= alt_indents[-1]:
                raise self._tab_error(line_no, scan - line_start)
            indents.append(column)
            alt_indents.append(alt_column)
            tokens.append(
                py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                    INDENT,
                    source[line_start:scan],
                    (line_no, 0),
                    (line_no, scan - line_start),
                    line_text,
                )
            )
        else:
            while column < indents[-1]:
                indents.pop()
                alt_indents.pop()
                tokens.append(
                    py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                        DEDENT,
                        "",
                        (line_no, scan - line_start),
                        (line_no, scan - line_start),
                        line_text,
                    )
                )
            if column != indents[-1]:
                raise OrmLexError(
                    code="E0001",
                    message="Unindent does not match any outer indentation level",
                    orm_line=line_no,
                    orm_col=scan - line_start + 1,
                    lang=self._adapter.lang,
                )
            if alt_column != alt_indents[-1]:
                raise self._tab_error(line_no, scan - line_start)
        return scan, line_no, line_start, False

    def _tab_error(self, line_no: int, col: int) -> OrmLexError:
        return OrmLexError(
            code="E0001",
            message="Inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation",
            orm_line=line_no,
            orm_col=col + 1,
            lang=self._adapter.lang,
        )

    # ── End of input ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    def _finish(
        self,
        tokens: list[py_tokenize.TokenInfo],
        brackets: list[tuple[str, int, int]],
        pending_newline: bool,
        indents: list[int],
        line_no: int,
        lines: list[str],
    ) -> list[py_tokenize.TokenInfo]:
        if brackets:
            char, open_line, open_col = brackets[-1]
            raise OrmLexError(
                code="E0001",
                message=f"'{char}' was never closed",
                orm_line=open_line,
                orm_col=open_col + 1,
                lang=self._adapter.lang,
            )
        # line_no is the line after the last one that was read, unless the
        # last line had no newline at its end.
        end_line = line_no if pending_newline else line_no - 1
        if pending_newline:
            col = len(lines[-1])
            tokens.append(
                py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                    NEWLINE, "", (end_line, col), (end_line, col + 1), ""
                )
            )
        for _ in indents[1:]:
            tokens.append(
                py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                    DEDENT, "", (end_line + 1, 0), (end_line + 1, 0), ""
                )
            )
        tokens.append(
            py_tokenize.TokenInfo(
                ENDMARKER, "", (end_line + 1, 0), (end_line + 1, 0), ""
            )
        )
        return tokens

    # ── Errors ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    def _raise_at(
        self, source: str, pos: int, line_no: int, line_start: int
    ) -> NoReturn:
        char = source[pos]
        if char in "\"'":
            message = "Unterminated string literal"
        else:
            message = f"Lexer error: {char!r}"
        raise OrmLexError(
            code="E0001",
            message=message,
            orm_line=line_no,
            orm_col=pos - line_start + 1,
            lang=self._adapter.lang,
        )

    # ── f-strings ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    def _translate_name(self, name: str) -> str:
        return self._combined_map.get(normalize_hudhaa(name), name)

    def _fail(self, message: str, source: str, pos: int) -> OrmLexError:
        line_no = source.count("\n", 0, pos) + 1
        col = pos - (source.rfind("\n", 0, pos) + 1)
        return OrmLexError(
            code="E0001",
            message=message,
            orm_line=line_no,
            orm_col=col + 1,
            lang=self._adapter.lang,
        )

    def _scan_fstring(self, source: str, pos: int) -> tuple[int, str]:
        """Scan an f-string that starts at ``pos``.

        Names inside ``{...}`` fields are translated. Fields may hold strings
        that use the same quote as the f-string (allowed since Python 3.12),
        so a plain regular expression cannot find the end of the literal.

        Returns:
            (index after the closing quote, translated literal text)
        """
        n = len(source)
        j = pos
        while source[j] not in "\"'":
            j += 1
        prefix = source[pos:j]
        raw = "r" in prefix or "R" in prefix
        quote = source[j]
        delim = quote * 3 if source.startswith(quote * 3, j) else quote
        k = j + len(delim)
        out = [source[pos:k]]
        while k < n:
            if source.startswith(delim, k):
                out.append(delim)
                return k + len(delim), "".join(out)
            ch = source[k]
            if ch == "\\":
                nxt = source[k + 1 : k + 2]
                if nxt in ("{", "}", ""):
                    out.append(ch)
                    k += 1
                elif nxt == "N" and not raw and source[k + 2 : k + 3] == "{":
                    close = source.find("}", k)
                    if close < 0:
                        break
                    out.append(source[k : close + 1])
                    k = close + 1
                else:
                    out.append(source[k : k + 2])
                    k += 2
            elif ch == "{":
                if source.startswith("{{", k):
                    out.append("{{")
                    k += 2
                else:
                    k = self._scan_field(source, k + 1, out, delim)
            elif ch == "\n" and len(delim) == 1:
                break
            else:
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
        raise self._fail("Unterminated string literal", source, pos)

    def _scan_field(self, source: str, k: int, out: list[str], delim: str) -> int:
        """Scan one replacement field; ``k`` is just after its ``{``.

        Appends the translated text, starting with the ``{``, to ``out`` and
        returns the index after the closing ``}``.
        """
        n = len(source)
        out.append("{")
        depth = 0
        in_spec = False
        seen_field = False
        while k < n:
            ch = source[k]
            if in_spec:
                if source.startswith(delim, k):
                    # The closing quote of the f-string ends it, also here.
                    raise self._fail("Unterminated f-string field", source, k)
                if ch == "{":
                    if seen_field and source.startswith("{{", k):
                        # Python 3.12: "{{" is an escape only after a field in
                        # the spec (see oromscript.fstrings).
                        out.append("{{")
                        k += 2
                    else:
                        k = self._scan_field(source, k + 1, out, delim)
                        seen_field = True
                    continue
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
                if ch == "}":
                    return k
                continue
            if ch in "\"'":
                end = self._skip_plain_string(source, k)
                out.append(source[k:end])
                k = end
            elif ch in "([{":
                depth += 1
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
            elif ch in ")]}":
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
                if depth == 0:
                    return k
                depth -= 1
            elif ch == ":" and depth == 0:
                in_spec = True
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
            elif ch == "!" and depth == 0 and source[k + 1 : k + 2] != "=":
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
                while k < n and source[k].isalpha():
                    out.append(source[k])
                    k += 1
            elif ch.isalpha() or ch == "_":
                k = self._scan_word(source, k, out)
            else:
                out.append(ch)
                k += 1
        raise self._fail("Unterminated f-string field", source, k - 1)

    def _scan_word(self, source: str, k: int, out: list[str]) -> int:
        """Translate the name at ``k`` inside an f-string field."""
        match = self._name_re.match(source, k)
        assert match is not None  # noqa: S101
        word = match.group()
        end = match.end()
        nxt = source[end : end + 1]
        if nxt in ("'", '"') and word.lower() in _STRING_PREFIXES:
            # A string with a prefix, for example rb"..." or f"..." in a field.
            if "f" in word.lower():
                string_end, text = self._scan_fstring(source, k)
                out.append(text)
                return string_end
            string_end = self._skip_plain_string(source, end)
            out.append(source[k:string_end])
            return string_end
        # A hudhaa inside a known keyword, for example walitti_ida'i
        while source[end : end + 1] in tuple(HUDHAA_VARIANTS):
            more = self._name_re.match(source, end + 1)
            if more is None:
                break
            candidate = word + HUDHAA + more.group()
            if normalize_hudhaa(candidate) not in self._combined_map:
                break
            word = candidate
            end = more.end()
        out.append(self._translate_name(word))
        return end

    @staticmethod
    def _skip_plain_string(source: str, k: int) -> int:
        """Return the index after the (non-f) string literal that starts at ``k``."""
        quote = source[k]
        delim = quote * 3 if source.startswith(quote * 3, k) else quote
        j = k + len(delim)
        n = len(source)
        while j < n:
            if source[j] == "\\":
                j += 2
            elif source.startswith(delim, j):
                return j + len(delim)
            else:
                j += 1
        return n

class OrmParser:
    """Parse a translated token stream into a Python AST.

    Args:
        adapter: The loaded Adapter for the active language.
    """

    def __init__(self, adapter: Adapter) -> None:
        self._adapter = adapter

    def parse(self, tokens: list[tokenize.TokenInfo]) -> ast.AST:
        """Convert tokens to AST.

        Args:
            tokens: Translated token list from OrmLexer.tokenize().

        Returns:
            A valid Python AST.

        Raises:
            OrmSyntaxError: If the source has a syntax error.
        """
        hooks = self._adapter.grammar_hooks
        hook = getattr(hooks, "pre_parse", None) if hooks is not None else None
        if hook is not None:
            # A hook works on source text, so it cannot see the token list.
            # If it changes the text, the standard parser reads the new text.
            source = tokenize.untokenize(tokens)
            new_source = hook(source)
            if new_source != source:
                return self._stdlib_parse(new_source)
        parser = _Parser(tokens, self._adapter)
        try:
            with gc_paused():
                return parser.parse_module()
        except RecursionError as exc:
            # Each level of brackets or blocks uses many Python frames.
            raise OrmSyntaxError(
                code="E0010",
                message="Too many levels of nesting",
                orm_line=parser._tok.start[0],
                orm_col=parser._tok.start[1] + 1,
                lang=self._adapter.lang,
                context={"text": parser._tok.line.rstrip("\n")},
            ) from exc

    def _stdlib_parse(self, source: str) -> ast.AST:
        try:
            return ast.parse(source, filename="<orm>", type_comments=False)
        except SyntaxError as exc:
            raise OrmSyntaxError(
                code="E0010",
                message=exc.msg,
                orm_line=exc.lineno or 0,
                orm_col=exc.offset or 0,
                lang=self._adapter.lang,
                context={"text": exc.text or ""},
            ) from exc

oromscript.graphemes ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Grapheme helpers for Afan Oromo (Qubee) text.

A grapheme here is one written unit of the language. Some units use more than one character:

  • digraphs: ch, dh, ny, ph, sh (and ts, zy)
  • long vowels: aa, ee, ii, oo, uu
  • doubled consonants: bb, kk, and doubled digraphs such as cch
  • the hudhaa (apostrophe) that marks a glottal stop, as in ba'e. It counts as a letter of its own.

A unit is written in one case (aa, AA) or capitalised (Aa, Ch). A mix such as aA is two units.

The lexer uses :func:normalize_hudhaa so that a keyword typed with a curly apostrophe still matches the keyword map. The other helpers are public tools for editors and error messages that need to count or cut words by letter.

class Grapheme(ast.AST):
    """A tree node for one written unit of an Afan Oromo word.

    ``text`` is the unit (``dh``, ``aa``, ``bb``, ``'``...). ``kind`` is one of
    ``geminate_digraph``, ``digraph``, ``long_vowel``, ``geminate``, ``hudhaa``,
    ``letter`` or ``other``. ``start`` and ``end`` are character offsets in the
    word (``end`` is exclusive).

    The parser attaches a tuple of these nodes to every name in the tree as the
    attribute ``graphemes``. The attribute is not one of the node's ``_fields``,
    so ``ast.walk``, ``ast.dump``, ``ast.unparse`` and ``compile`` ignore it.
    Use :func:`iter_graphemes` to find them.
    """

    _fields = ("text", "kind", "start", "end")
    text: str
    kind: str
    start: int
    end: int

    def __init__(
        self, text: str = "", kind: str = "other", start: int = 0, end: int = 0
    ) -> None:
        self.text = text
        self.kind = kind
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    @property
    def is_multi_character(self) -> bool:
        """True for digraphs, long vowels and doubled consonants."""
        return self.kind in MULTI_CHARACTER_KINDS

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=4096)
def grapheme_nodes(word: str) -> tuple[Grapheme, ...]:
    """Return the :class:`Grapheme` nodes of ``word``.

    A combining mark stays attached to the unit before it. The result is
    cached, so every use of the same name shares the same nodes. Do not
    change them.

    >>> [g.text for g in grapheme_nodes("dhaabbata")]
    ['dh', 'aa', 'bb', 'a', 't', 'a']
    """
    nodes: list[Grapheme] = []
    for match in _GRAPHEME_RE.finditer(word):
        piece = match.group(0)
        kind = match.lastgroup or "other"
        if kind == "other":
            if piece in HUDHAA_VARIANTS:
                kind = "hudhaa"
            elif piece.isalpha():
                kind = "letter"
        if nodes and unicodedata.combining(piece[0]):
            last = nodes[-1]
            nodes[-1] = Grapheme(
                text=last.text + piece,
                kind=last.kind,
                start=last.start,
                end=match.end(),
            )
        else:
            nodes.append(
                Grapheme(text=piece, kind=kind, start=match.start(), end=match.end())
            )
    return tuple(nodes)

def iter_graphemes(tree: ast.AST) -> Iterator[tuple[ast.AST, tuple[Grapheme, ...]]]:
    """Yield ``(node, graphemes)`` for every named node in ``tree``.

    Works on any tree. If the parser did not attach graphemes, they are made now.
    """
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        field = _NAME_FIELDS.get(type(node))
        if field is None:
            continue
        name = getattr(node, field, None)
        if not name:
            continue
        found = getattr(node, "graphemes", None)
        yield node, found if found is not None else grapheme_nodes(name)

class SemanticAnalyser(ast.NodeVisitor):
    """Analyse and annotate an AST.

    Args:
        source_lines: Original .orm source split by line (for error context).
        strict: If True, raise OrmNameError on undefined name references.
    """

    def __init__(self, source_lines: list[str], strict: bool = False) -> None:
        self._lines = source_lines
        self._strict = strict
        self._scope: _Scope = _Scope()
        self._orm_line_map: dict[int, int] = {}  # ast node id → orm_line

    def analyse(self, tree: ast.AST) -> tuple[ast.AST, SourceMap]:
        """Run analysis pass.

        Returns:
            (annotated_tree, source_map) where source_map maps
            each AST node's lineno to the original orm line number.
        """
        self.visit(tree)
        return tree, self._orm_line_map

    # ── Visitors ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    def visit_FunctionDef(self, node: ast.FunctionDef) -> None:
        self._scope[node.name] = "function"
        self._scope = self._scope.new_child()
        for arg in node.args.args:
            self._scope[arg.arg] = "arg"
        self.generic_visit(node)
        self._scope = self._scope.parents

    visit_AsyncFunctionDef = visit_FunctionDef  # type: ignore[assignment]

    def visit_ClassDef(self, node: ast.ClassDef) -> None:
        self._scope[node.name] = "class"
        self._scope = self._scope.new_child()
        self.generic_visit(node)
        self._scope = self._scope.parents

    def visit_Assign(self, node: ast.Assign) -> None:
        for target in node.targets:
            if isinstance(target, ast.Name):
                self._scope[target.id] = "var"
        self.generic_visit(node)

    def visit_Name(self, node: ast.Name) -> None:
        if (
            self._strict
            and isinstance(node.ctx, ast.Load)
            and node.id not in self._scope
            and node.id not in dir(__builtins__)
        ):
            from .errors import OrmNameError

            raise OrmNameError(
                code="E0020",
                message=f"Name '{node.id}' is not defined",
                orm_line=getattr(node, "lineno", 0),
                orm_col=getattr(node, "col_offset", 0),
                lang="",
                context={"name": node.id},
            )

class AdapterRegistry:
    """Global registry of available language adapters."""

    _adapters: dict[str, Adapter] = {}

    @classmethod
    def discover(cls, adapters_dir: Path) -> None:
        """Scan adapters_dir and register all found adapters."""
        for d in adapters_dir.iterdir():
            if (
                d.is_dir()
                and (d / "keyword_map.json").exists()
                and d.name not in cls._adapters
            ):
                cls._adapters[d.name] = Adapter.load(d)

    @classmethod
    def get(cls, lang: str) -> Adapter:
        if lang not in cls._adapters:
            raise OrmAdapterError(
                code="E0051",
                message=f"No adapter found for language '{lang}'. "
                f"Available: {list(cls._adapters)}",
                lang=lang,
            )
        return cls._adapters[lang]

    @classmethod
    def list_langs(cls) -> list[str]:
        return sorted(cls._adapters.keys())

def discover(cls, adapters_dir: Path) -> None:
    """Scan adapters_dir and register all found adapters."""
    for d in adapters_dir.iterdir():
        if (
            d.is_dir()
            and (d / "keyword_map.json").exists()
            and d.name not in cls._adapters
        ):
            cls._adapters[d.name] = Adapter.load(d)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The OromScript transpiler pipeline is designed to be fully standard-compliant with modern Python, meaning its output is standard Python code. The pipeline consists of the following core stages:

  1. Lexer (oromscript.lexer): A hand-written lexer. It splits the source into tokens, tracks indentation, and replaces local-language names with Python names (e.g., hojii -> def).
  2. Parser (oromscript.parser): A hand-written recursive descent parser. It turns the token stream into a standard Python Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
  3. Semantic Analysis (oromscript.semantic): Validates the AST and prepares source-map information.
  4. Code Generation (oromscript.codegen): Traverses the AST to reconstruct perfectly formatted Python source code using ast.unparse.

A fifth module, oromscript.graphemes, holds helpers for Afan Oromo letters. The lexer uses it to accept every kind of apostrophe.

For a full breakdown of the system design, read the OromScript Design Specification.

docs.title: Lexer
docs.text:
The lexer reads the whole source with one compiled regular expression. It does not use Python's tokenize module. It produces standard tokenize.TokenInfo objects, so other tools can read its output.

What it does:

  • Tokens. Names, numbers (hex, octal, binary, floats, imaginary, underscores), strings (all prefixes, triple quotes, escapes), operators, and comments.
  • Layout. It emits NEWLINE, INDENT, and DEDENT tokens. A tab counts as up to the next multiple of 8 columns. Blank lines and comment-only lines do not change indentation. Newlines inside brackets and after a backslash do not end a statement.
  • Translation. A name found in the adapter's keyword or builtin map is replaced by the Python name. Names inside strings and comments are never changed.
  • Positions. Each token keeps its line and column in the original .orm source, even after translation. Errors point at the original text.
  • f-strings. Names inside the {...} fields of an f-string are translated. Text outside the fields and the format specifications are left alone. Strings that reuse the outer quote inside a field (Python 3.12 style) work.
  • Hudhaa. Some Afan Oromo words contain an apostrophe, such as walitti_ida'i. The lexer matches these words and also accepts the curly apostrophes ’, ʼ, and ‘, because many keyboards produce them.
  • Identifiers. Names that are not plain ASCII are normalised to NFKC form, as Python does. A character that cannot be in a name is an error.
  • Byte order mark. A leading byte order mark (U+FEFF) is ignored. Python's ast.parse rejects it in text, but editors on Windows often add it to UTF-8 files.
  • Differences from tokenize. The tokens equal tokenize for ordinary Python, with these exceptions: \r\n and lone \r become \n, a leading byte order mark is dropped, non-ASCII names are NFKC-normalised, f-strings are one STRING token (as tokenize does before Python 3.12), and an invalid number such as 0x or 1__0 is split into separate tokens that the parser then rejects.
  • Errors. Problems raise OrmLexError with code E0001: an unterminated string (an unterminated """ is never read as an empty string), a character that is not valid, a NUL byte anywhere, an unclosed bracket (the message names the bracket and points at it), an indentation level that matches no outer level, mixed tabs and spaces that Python would reject, and a backslash at the very end of the file.

Line and column numbers in lexer and parser errors both start at 1.

The lexer follows the rules of CPython's own tokenizer, including odd ones: a backslash inside the indentation fixes the indentation level, and a backslash followed by spaces at the end of the file is accepted.

docs.title: Parser
docs.text:
The parser is a recursive descent parser. Each grammar rule is one method. Binary operators use precedence climbing, which keeps the number of calls per expression small.

  • It covers the Python grammar of the Python version that runs it: all statements, expressions, comprehensions, lambdas, decorators, async, match statements with every pattern kind, parenthesised with items, and, where that Python allows them, except*, starred subscripts, type parameters and type aliases. Newer syntax is rejected on older Python, as ast.parse does.
  • match and case are soft keywords. The parser tries a match statement first and falls back to treating match as a normal name, so match = 1 still works.
  • Every node gets lineno, col_offset, end_lineno, and end_col_offset, set from the tokens. Columns count characters, not UTF-8 bytes.
  • f-strings are cut into text and fields by oromscript.fstrings. Each field expression is read by the same lexer and parser. The result follows CPython's rules for the Python version that runs it: from 3.12 a field may hold the outer quote, backslashes, comments and newlines, and format specs may nest one level deeper. Every node inside an f-string carries the position of the whole string.
  • Plain string literals are decoded by oromscript.strings, not by ast.literal_eval. A bad escape such as "\d" gives a warning that names the .orm line, and no global warning filter is changed, so it is safe to use from threads.
  • Speed. The parser reuses one object for each context and operator (as CPython does), skips the or, and and comparison levels for simple operands, and pauses Python's cycle collector while it builds the tree (oromscript._gc).
  • Code nested too deeply for the Python stack (about 70 levels of brackets, depending on the call stack) raises OrmSyntaxError instead of RecursionError.
  • Errors raise OrmSyntaxError with code E0010, the line, the column, and the source text of the line.
  • If an adapter's grammar_hooks.pre_parse changes the source text, the parser reads the changed text with Python's own ast.parse. Any hook makes the parser rebuild the whole source text first, which takes about 8% of the parse time, so define one only if it changes something. The Afan Oromo adapter defines none.
  • Python 3.14 template strings (t"...") are not supported.

docs.title: Graphemes
docs.text:
oromscript.graphemes knows how Afan Oromo (Qubee) letters are written:

Kind Examples Digraphs (digraph) ch, dh, ny, ph, sh, ts, zy Long vowels (long_vowel) aa, ee, ii, oo, uu Doubled consonants (geminate) bb, kk Doubled digraphs (geminate_digraph) cch, ddh Hudhaa (hudhaa) ', ’, ʼ, ‘

A unit is written in one case (aa, AA) or capitalised (Aa, Ch).

from oromscript import split_graphemes, grapheme_len

split_graphemes("dhaabbata")   # ['dh', 'aa', 'bb', 'a', 't', 'a']
grapheme_len("dhaabbata")      # 6

docs.title: Grapheme nodes in the syntax tree
docs.text:
Grapheme is an ast.AST node with the fields text, kind, start and end (offsets in the name). The parser attaches a tuple of them to every Name, Attribute, arg, keyword, FunctionDef, AsyncFunctionDef, ClassDef, ExceptHandler and alias as the attribute graphemes:

from oromscript.graphemes import iter_graphemes

for node, graphemes in iter_graphemes(tree):
    print(type(node).__name__, [g.text for g in graphemes if g.is_multi_character])
# arg ['dh', 'aa', 'bb']

graphemes is not one of the node's _fields, so ast.walk, ast.dump, ast.unparse and compile ignore it and the tree stays valid Python. Equal names share the same cached nodes, so do not change them. The nodes describe names as they stand in the tree, so a translated keyword shows its Python name (print, not agarsiisi).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The lexer and parser are checked against Python itself:

  • The parser's tree and node positions are compared with ast.parse on hundreds of snippets, and on a sample of the Python standard library.
  • The lexer's tokens are compared with tokenize on plain Python source.
  • Invalid programs must be rejected by both parsers.
  • Memory tests (tests/test_memory.py) run the pipeline many times and fail if memory or object counts grow.
  • Speed tests (tests/test_performance.py) check throughput and that time grows in line with file size.

Run everything with make test. Run the full standard library comparison with pytest -m slow. Run the benchmark with make bench.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
python benchmarks/bench.py prints the time for each stage. On a development laptop (Python 3.14), measured on two 1 MB files:

File Tokens Lexer Parser Lexer + parser Print statements (35,000 lines) 175,000 0.27 to 0.33 s 0.25 to 0.37 s 250,000 to 330,000 tokens/sec Mixed code from examples/ 215,000 0.37 to 0.48 s 0.30 to 0.45 s 230,000 to 320,000 tokens/sec

The first figure in each range is the best of several runs, and the second is the mean of three runs in benchmarks/bench.py on a busy desktop. The whole transpile of a 1 MB file, including semantic analysis and code generation, takes about 1.2 to 1.3 seconds. The numbers depend on the machine and vary by about 20% from run to run.

docs.title: Contributing to OromScript
docs.text: We welcome contributions of all forms—bug reports, feature requests, new language adapters, and code contributions.

docs.title: Contribution Workflow
docs.text:
1. Fork & Clone the repository.
  2. Branching:
  3. feat/ for new features or keywords
  4. fix/ for bug fixes
  5. lang/ for new language adapters
  6. docs/ for documentation
  7. chore/ for tooling and deps
  8. Make changes and ensure make test runs cleanly.
  9. Open a Pull Request to the main branch.

docs.title: Adding a New Language Adapter
docs.text:
Using OromScript's plugin infrastructure, it's easy to add a new language. You primarily need to supply a JSON keyword map and an error messages set.

  1. Scaffold: oromscript new-lang amharic (for Amharic)
  2. Translate Keywords: Edit adapters/<lang>/keyword_map.json mapping each Python keyword/builtin to local equivalents.
  3. Localize Errors: Fill error_messages.json with appropriate translated syntax errors.
  4. Test Corpus: Add testing .orm and expected .py pairs in adapters/<lang>/tests/corpus/
  5. Validate Schema: Run oromscript validate-adapter adapters/<lang>/
  6. Submit PR.

docs.title: Testing & Coverage
docs.text:
• We require 100% of keywords in keyword_map.json to have at least one corpus test.
  • Every mapped error path should trigger properly in tests.
  • Core engine coverage requirement is ≥ 90% (CI requires 95%).
  • Changes to oromscript/lexer.py or oromscript/parser.py must keep the comparison tests with CPython passing (tests/test_lexer.py, tests/test_parser.py). Add a snippet to the VALID or INVALID list for every new case.
  • Run make test-slow to compare the parser with the whole Python standard library.
  • Run make bench before and after a change that could affect speed. tests/test_memory.py fails if a change makes memory or object counts grow.

For more details on the architecture, see Architecture and Design Specification.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Welcome to OromScript! This guide will help you install and run your first OromScript program.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You can install OromScript locally for development:

git clone https://github.com/ayanasamuel8/transpiler-afan-oromo-script.git
cd transpiler-afan-oromo-script
pip install -e .

docs.title: Running a Program
docs.text:
Create a file named hello.orm with the following content:

agarsiisi("Akkam, Addunyaa!")

Then run it using the OromScript CLI:

oromscript run hello.orm
